analysis.one_liner: Funds free lawyers for low-income tenants facing eviction and creates a national eviction database.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would pay for lawyers for very low-income tenants in eviction court, never received a hearing or a vote in either chamber before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would authorize $125 million a year, for five years, in grants to states and cities to hire attorneys dedicated to representing tenants in eviction cases, with eligibility limited to people living below 125% of the federal poverty level. It would also require HUD to build the first national database of evictions, tracking who is evicted, why, and whether tenants had lawyers, and direct the Government Accountability Office to study how representation affects case outcomes. Its purpose is to level a courtroom playing field where landlords almost always have counsel and tenants usually do not.
analysis.who_benefits: Tenants living below 125% of the federal poverty level who are facing eviction would gain access to a free attorney — an advantage that in eviction court strongly affects whether someone keeps their home. States and cities would get funding to build or expand right-to-counsel programs, and courts and researchers would gain data on evictions that does not currently exist anywhere at the national level.

how_it_helps.text: Authorizes the Attorney General to make grants, at least $1 million each, to states and local governments to hire attorneys dedicated solely to representing eligible tenants in eviction cases, with $125 million authorized for each of fiscal years 2022 through 2026.
Limits eligibility to individuals whose income is below 125% of the federal poverty level, targeting the help at the poorest tenants.

Requires HUD to establish a national database of court-ordered, administrative, and illegal evictions, including case outcomes, whether the tenant had a lawyer, household composition, and data on illegal lockouts, with privacy safeguards for domestic violence victims.

Directs the GAO to report to Congress on the national status of legal representation of tenants in eviction cases, the effect of representation on default rates and case outcomes, and potential cost savings from providing counsel.

analysis.who_pays: Landlords and property owners would bear the main cost: evictions would become slower, harder, and more expensive when tenants have counsel, and the national database would track landlords by name, how often they file, and what they allege tenants owe. Taxpayers would fund the $125 million annual grant program plus $5 million a year for the database, and state courts and clerks would take on new data-reporting duties.

drawbacks.text: The program is funded only through appropriations — the grants exist in law only if Congress actually appropriates the money each year, and the bill includes no dedicated revenue source.

To qualify for a grant, a state or locality without a right-to-counsel law must show the Attorney General evidence of 'substantial progress' toward enacting such a law, which could exclude some high-need places from getting help.

The database would require state attorneys general, courts, and court clerks to collect and submit detailed data on every eviction case, a new administrative burden that could strain local court systems.

Adding lawyers to eviction cases can slow the process and raise costs for landlords, including small landlords, not just large corporate ones; landlords would also lose some of the leverage that comes from tenants appearing in court unrepresented.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete: a lawyer in an eviction case can be the difference between keeping a home and a default judgment, and the bill targets that help at the very poorest tenants while building the first national evidence base on evictions. The costs are real but comparatively modest — a $130 million annual authorization is small by federal standards, and the main parties paying are landlords, whose interest in fast, uncontested evictions is exactly what the bill is designed to counter. The strongest fair criticisms are the appropriations-only funding and the gatekeeping requirement that states show progress toward a right-to-counsel law before receiving grants.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Financial Services and Judiciary committees when it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote in either chamber before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rosa DeLauro (D-CT) introduced the bill on May 28, 2021, and it was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and, in addition, the House Judiciary Committee.
The bill attracted 68 cosponsors, all Democrats.

Sixteen months after introduction, the only further action was a referral to the Judiciary Committee's Subcommittee on the Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties on November 1, 2022 — near the end of the Congress.
No committee hearing, markup, or floor vote ever occurred in the House, and the bill was never introduced in the Senate.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Landlords and property owners came out ahead: no lawyer program was funded and no national database of evictions was created, so evictions remain as fast, cheap, and uncontested as before. The 68 cosponsoring House Democrats gained nothing for their constituents.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

against.name: House Financial Services and Judiciary Committees
against.what_they_did: Held the bill without any hearing, markup, or vote; the only action in the Judiciary Committee was a referral to a subcommittee sixteen months after introduction.

against.name: House Republican conference
against.what_they_did: Offered no cosponsor or recorded support for the bill.

sides.party_line_note: Support was entirely Democratic: all 68 cosponsors were House Democrats, with no Republican cosponsors, and the bill died in committee without any recorded vote that would have shown broader positions.

industries.note: The bill would give tenants in eviction cases the same professional representation landlords almost always have, making evictions slower, costlier, and more likely to end with the tenant staying. It would also log each landlord's eviction filings and alleged debts in a national database. The bill died, so landlords avoided both.

industries.industry: Civil legal aid and the legal services industry
industries.note: The bill would have created a dedicated funding stream requiring states and cities to hire attorneys solely to represent poor tenants in eviction cases. That work did not get funded, so legal aid groups continue to turn away most eligible tenants.

A national eviction database with strict privacy safeguards could have reduced reliance on the patchwork of private screening reports that often contain errors, but the bill kept its detailed data inside HUD with access rules, so its effect on that market is indirect either way.
